title: Fennel and Celery Slaw
subtitle: Crisp shaved fennel and celery with a lemon creme fraiche dressing
excerpt: Thinly shaved fennel and finely sliced celery in a light lemon and creme fraiche dressing with dill. A delicate, anise-scented slaw that works alongside fish, seafood or cold poultry.
sourceNotes: Fennel slaw with creamy dressings appears across Scandinavian and British contemporary cooking traditions, building on the fennel-and-celery combination used in French cuisine. The creme fraiche dressing, sharpened with lemon, is a lighter alternative to mayonnaise and pairs particularly well with fish and seafood.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made 15 to 30 minutes before serving. The fennel softens as it sits; do not make more than 2 hours ahead.

content.text: Fennel and celery slaw works because both ingredients share a clean, fresh, slightly anise quality that is lighter than cabbage, and they both crisp well when very thinly shaved. Paired with a creme fraiche and lemon dressing and fresh dill, the result is a slaw that suits fish much better than a heavy mayo version. This is the slaw to serve with smoked salmon, poached fish or cold roast chicken.

items.prepNote: outer layers removed, very thinly shaved

content.text: Combine the shaved fennel, sliced celery and spring onion in a large bowl. Stir together {{creme-fraiche}} of creme fraiche, the juice of {{lemon}} lemon, {{dijon-mustard}} of Dijon mustard, {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of pepper. Pour the dressing over the vegetables and toss to coat. Add the dill and any reserved celery leaves and toss again. Leave for 15 minutes before serving.

items.fix: Use a mandoline or very sharp knife to shave the fennel as thin as possible. Thick fennel is tough and the anise flavour is aggressive; thin fennel is delicate.

items.cause: Fennel releases water as it sits.
items.fix: Dress the slaw close to serving and serve within 2 hours. If made ahead without dressing, keep the components dry and combine at the last moment.

content.text: Fennel slaw has appeared on British menus as an alternative to cabbage coleslaw since the 1990s, mostly alongside fish. The fennel and dill combination comes from Scandinavian cooking; the creme fraiche dressing from French tradition. The result suits fish and seafood better than a cabbage slaw.
